newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down after strong 5-year auction.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down after strong 5-year auction.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Wednesday after a strong five-year Treasury note auction failed to attact followthrough demand in the secondary market, analysts said.
The U.S. Treasury sold $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday with the high yield a better than expected 7.45 pct.
The ratio of bids offered to those accepted was 2.58 to one, higher than usual for the intermediate-term maturity. And non-competitive bids totaled a strong $667 million, the Treasury said.

The market ticked up about an eighth of a point after the favorable auction results. But when the dealers who bought the new securities could not unload them, Treasury prices were adjusted downward in an attempt to find buyers, analysts said.

"The market didn't look too bad going into the auction but the bottom line is that the dealers who took down the auction tried to flip it and there was nobody on the other side of that trade," said one trader.
"The lack of followthrough after the auction caused some selling," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.

"The good auction results were more apparent than real," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and fixed-income research director at Dean Witter Reynolds. "The Street found itself with more paper than it wanted and there was no followthrough demand in the secondary market so they began to push prices down in thin trading."
Analysts said headlines coming out of the U.S. budget talks might also have been negative for bonds on Wednesday.
U.S. Treasuries ended higher on Tuesday, partly buoyed by hopes for an agreement between the Clinton administration and Republican leaders on a balanced budget.
But those hopes appeared not to bear fruit on Wednesday.
"There was some profit-taking off of that," he said.

Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank President Jack Guynn, speaking at a Chamber of Commerce luncheon in Murfreesboro, Tenn., said the Fed's monetary policy must be pre-emptive and that consumer demand presents the largest upside risk to the U.S. economy.
Analysts said Guynn's remarks were not market movers.
"We've been hearing that over and over again," said Stiles. "There's nothing terribly surprising about (those comments)."
Analysts said investors also had to consider that the bond market was near the top of its range for the month -- just a week away from some very influential economic data.

The first-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), said to be favored by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, is due on Tuesday. The first-quarter real GDP number is due a day later. The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) April survey is due on May 1 and April U.S. employment data are due on May 2.
"The market is near the high of the month's range ahead of all the big data," said Stiles. "So you could see it was vulnerable."
